chapter: Sidemen, mixed bands, the Apollo and Lena Horne
title: Howard McGhee joins the band
summary: McGhee was hired in New York around 1943-44 as a modern trumpeter alongside Peanuts Holland and Al Killian, and left when Barnet disbanded because of the draft board.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Okay, we got that one straightened out. How about Howard McGee, how did he happen to get in your band?
Well, we needed a trumpet player and Howard's a good trumpet player, and so we hired him.
That was where?
That was in New York. I think that was about '43, maybe early '44, and Howard wrote a couple of

charts for us. One of them we recorded, it was called, "Strolling". And he was a much more modern style trumpet player than Peanuts Holland, and this was an attempt in a way, you know, to have more of a variety of styles of trumpet players, because Peanuts was the traditional type trumpeter.
They were in the band at the same time?
Oh, yeah.
That's what I thought.

He and Al Killian. Al Killian was still there part of the time. But at that time I think we were using five trumpets, which it seems to me we were. Anyway, the reason for it was we wanted a guy that was playing in a more modern idiom. He was into the Dizzy Gillespie bag and --
Yeah, a bopper.
Yeah. And so we got Howard.
How long was he in the band?
Well, he was with the band until I just couldn't stand these -- when I broke the band up on account of these appearances before the draft board, I just -- it was really unnerving, you know.
Sure.
It was like somebody -- you're standing on a rug and waiting for somebody to pull it out from underneath you. So it wasn't that he got fired. I just disbanded the

whole band. And of course Howard went on, he made quite a mark for himself. Unfortunately he was ill with some things that a lot of the guys got into, which was a shame, because I always thought that Howard could play as good as anybody when he was right. He's still here, though.
Yeah.
And that's --
Yeah, I saw him conducting last year, in Los Angeles.
Well, good.
I don't know whether he's playing much, but --
Well, of course Howard's got to be up there now. We're talking back '43, here we are in '78. This is 35 years ago.
Dizzy's still playing, though.
Oh, yes, he is.
